svg.title: The four counter-intuitive truths about security design, each with the belief it replaces
svg.desc: Four cards. One: security is not a zone but a relationship chain - it exists only at the point where two entities with different trust levels interact, so the first deliverable is a trust boundary inventory, not a device list. Two: encryption solves cannot-see, not cannot-get-in - a VPN gives confidentiality and peer authentication but no authorization, no content inspection and no lateral movement control, so a fully meshed IPsec network still lets one compromised PC move sideways. Three: the cost of security is not in buying but in changing processes - in an 802.1X project procurement and configuration take about 30 percent and the other 70 percent goes to the printer that does not support it, the medical vendor that refuses to cooperate, visitor access, the fallback when the authentication server dies, and who is on call. Four: default deny is easy to say, the hard part is who owns the whitelist - who submits, who approves, how long until it takes effect, and who removes it when the business is gone. A footer states that a design without a trust boundary inventory is a collage of product brochures.
svg.text: Four truths that invalidate the usual security diagram
Each card carries the belief it replaces - that is the part people argue with, not the technology.
TRUTH 1
Security is an edge, not a surface
the belief: draw a box called "secure zone" around the core
Security exists only where two entities with different
trust levels interact. It is a line between them, and
a box drawn on a diagram enforces nothing.
Deliverable: the list of flows crossing each boundary
no boundary inventory = a collage of product brochures
TRUTH 2
Encryption hides, it does not admit
the belief: "we have IPsec everywhere, so we are secure"
A VPN gives confidentiality and peer authentication.
It does not authorize, does not inspect content, and
does not stop lateral movement inside the tunnel.
One compromised PC moves through the whole mesh
and every packet looks like a legitimate encrypted session
TRUTH 3
The cost is process, not hardware
the belief: buy the platform, configure it, done
In an 802.1X project, procurement plus configuration is
about 30 percent. The other 70 is the printer that cannot
authenticate and the vendor who will not cooperate.
30%: buy and configure
70%: exceptions, fallback, on-call
TRUTH 4
Default deny needs an owner
the belief: "just default deny everything"
Who submits the request when a new business goes live?
Who approves it, how fast, and who deletes the rule when
the project is over? Unanswered, default deny is bypassed
by shadow rules and the policy dies of its own exceptions.
A rule with no expiry date is a rule forever
The four truths share one consequence: the deliverable of a security design is a set of relationships and processes, not a rack diagram.
Every time a design document jumps straight to "we will deploy a firewall", one of these four is being skipped.
